prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators

statement.case_for: After reading the colleagues' ballots I still put topological insulators first. The discovery has the structure I trust most: a simple, general model (Kane-Mele, with the Z2 invariant and protected helical edge states) that can be analysed exactly and carries a sharp, falsifiable prediction, followed by a decisive experiment (Molenkamp's HgTe quantum wells) that confirmed the quantised edge conductance. It has since been confirmed in several independent materials and probes, and the idea has migrated to photonic, acoustic and cold-atom systems, which is a good sign that a real mechanism has been identified and not just a material. The 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions and the Haldane and TKNN lineage, but the Z2 classification and time-reversal-protected topology in spin-orbit-coupled materials are a distinct, later step. Nobody on the committee disputes the physics, and the supplied credit forms a theory-plus-experiment trio that maps onto the actual record.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are attribution and overlap. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp's experiment tested, and Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore and Balents, and Hasan and colleagues, are central to the three-dimensional story. Any three-person set leaves a serious claim outside it, and a citation worded around the quantum spin Hall effect alone leaves the 3D case to a later prize or to none. There is also the argument that the 2016 prize already covered much of the conceptual ground, and that applications are still limited. I take the overlap objection seriously but think it fails on the science, and I take the attribution objection as the real weak point of my own first choice.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, valuing a band-structure prediction followed by direct experimental realisation, and ranked topological insulators third with the 2016 overlap and the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit as complications.
responses.response: I agree that the theory-meets-measurement structure is the right test and that both candidates pass it. Where we differ is maturity. For twisted bilayer graphene the pairing mechanism is unsettled, the phase diagram is sensitive to twist-angle disorder, and the field is under ten years old, so we do not yet understand what was discovered. For topological insulators the interpretation has been stable for fifteen years. On the overlap, I read 2016 as the topology of many-body and Chern-type phases, whereas Z2 topology protected by time-reversal symmetry is a separate classification. I do share your worry about Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, and that is the real cost of my preference.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked optical lattice clocks first for their clean, well-understood atomic physics and ranked topological insulators third, noting that attribution is contested among several theorists and experimentalists.
responses.response: The clocks are an excellent candidate and I ranked them eighth only on novelty, not quality. I would put clocks as my fallback. Lindroth is right that the attribution here is contested, and I cannot fully rebut it. But the contest is about whether to add names to a core that is itself well defined, namely Kane and Mele for the Z2 theory and Molenkamp for the first observation. The clock credit is cleaner on names, but it sits closer to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, and impact beyond metrology is still prospective, which matters for a prize about discovery.

responses.point: Johansson ranked optical lattice clocks first as a highly mature, clean precision system, and deferred to condensed-matter colleagues on topological insulators, flagging the missing HgTe theorists and the 3D contributors.
responses.response: I accept the attribution flags, and they are the reason I would not call the topological insulator allocation settled. On the ranking, Johansson's own argument for clocks, that the field is mature and independently reproduced, applies at least as strongly to topological insulators, which have been confirmed through transport and ARPES in many materials. I disagree with the framing that lattice clocks are the natural next step after the 2005 prize: that is an argument from continuity of method, whereas I would weigh the discovery of a new class of quantum matter more heavily than a further gain in precision.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranked IceCube first for opening a new observational window and valued detector-based achievements, and ranked the lattice clocks second.
responses.response: I respect the argument that a new window deserves weight, and IceCube's diffuse-flux detection is solid. My reservation is attribution and maturity of the science that was opened. The credited pair leaves out the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers, the origin of the flux is largely unresolved, and only a few individual sources are known. A prize recognises what we now understand, and I find the topological story more complete on that score. I do not want to push this too hard, since it is a difference of weighting, not of facts.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can defend a prize that omits Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu, given that only the supplied names can be credited.
How far the 2016 topological-phase prize reduces the novelty of the Z2 and quantum spin Hall step in colleagues' eyes.
Whether lattice clocks, with the broadest opening support, should take precedence in a one-prize year; my knowledge of priority details is from memory and not independently verified.
Whether a two-part prize combining a condensed-matter and an AMO achievement would be preferable, which the three-person limit makes hard with the supplied credits.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the candidates on the shortlist. I have no known collaboration with Kane, Mele or Molenkamp, or with the lattice-clock or cold-atom candidates. I work in the same Gothenburg physics environment as colleagues Johansson and Olsson, but this is an institutional fact and not a recusal issue for my preferred configuration.
